title: How do you avoid writing a separate pipeline for every one of thousands of microservices: Jenkins Shared Libraries (reusable Groovy steps in a versioned repo) and generic parameterized/templated pipelines (one `Jenkinsfile` + per-service config): and how do you trigger the right environment pipeline per branch (dev→Dev, qa→QA) with approvals/gates before Prod?
shortTitle: Avoiding a Separate Pipeline per Microservice: Shared Libraries, Templated Pipelines, and Per-Branch Environment Routing
keyPoints: A Jenkins Shared Library is a versioned Git repository with reusable Groovy steps under vars/ and structured classes under src/.
One library step like bankPipeline contains the entire standard pipeline, and each service's Jenkinsfile shrinks to two lines.
Per-service variation comes from a small config file like bank-ci.yaml loaded by the template with readYaml.
Branch-to-environment routing maps env.BRANCH_NAME to a target namespace so every service routes consistently.
The Prod deploy stage has an input approval gate restricted by submitter and wrapped in a timeout.
Pinning the library to a version tag gives reproducibility and an audit trail across all services.

s1_definition.oneliner: One versioned Shared Library plus a tiny per-service config replaces thousands of copy-pasted pipelines, and the branch name decides the environment with an approval gate before Prod.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Shared Library** – a versioned Git repository with reusable Groovy steps (`vars/`) and classes (`src/`), loaded with `@Library`.
- **Templated pipeline** – the entire standard pipeline lives in one library step; each microservice's Jenkinsfile calls it with per-service parameters.
- **Per-service config** – a small file like `bank-ci.yaml` checked into each service repo, read by the template with `readYaml`.
- **Branch-to-environment routing** – the template maps `env.BRANCH_NAME` to a target namespace (dev branch to Dev, qa to QA, main to Prod).
- **Approval gate** – an `input` step restricted by `submitter` to named release managers, wrapped in a `timeout`.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India has thousands of branches, and nobody writes a separate operations manual for each one. Instead there is one master manual at head office (the Shared Library), and every branch has a one-page cover sheet saying its name and manager. When head office improves a procedure, every branch gets it. Which counter a cheque goes to depends on the door: the dev door routes to the practice counter, the qa door to testing, and the main vault needs a manager's signature.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Shared Library repo (bank-shared-lib)
  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
  │  vars/bankPipeline.groovy        │  ← Full pipeline template
  │  vars/bankDeploy.groovy          │  ← Reusable deploy step
  │  src/com/bank/ci/Scanner.groovy  │  ← Structured classes
  └─────────────────────────────────┘
           │
           │  @Library('bank-shared-lib@v3') _
           ▼
  ┌──────────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────────┐
  │ transfer-service      │  │ fraud-service         │
  │ Jenkinsfile (2 lines) │  │ Jenkinsfile (2 lines) │
  │ bank-ci.yaml          │  │ bank-ci.yaml          │
  └──────────────────────┘  └──────────────────────┘

  Branch-to-environment routing:

  dev branch  ───▶  Dev namespace   (no gate)
  qa  branch  ───▶  QA  namespace   (no gate)
  main branch ───▶  Prod namespace  (approval gate)
                         │
                    ┌────┴────┐
                    │  input   │
                    │ submitter│
                    │ release- │
                    │ managers │
                    └─────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
To avoid maintaining hundreds of near-identical pipelines, I centralize the pipeline logic in a Jenkins Shared Library. The entire standard pipeline lives in one library step, and each microservice keeps a tiny two-line Jenkinsfile that loads the library and calls that step. When the security team mandates a new scan, I add it once to the template and every service picks it up on the next build.

Environment routing is driven by the branch name and owned by the template. A push to dev deploys to the Dev namespace, qa to QA, and main to Prod. Production is protected by an approval gate with input restricted to named release managers and wrapped in a timeout, so no service can skip it.

Governance is the senior concern. I pin the library to a version tag so every service gets a known, audited version. Library changes go through their own code review and tests, because a bug in the shared library breaks every service at once. I validate per-service config and reject unknown keys, because the template runs with broad permissions.

Remember one sentence: one versioned Shared Library plus a tiny per-service config replaces thousands of copy-pasted pipelines.
